# Job Chapter 19 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic)
**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Leningrad Codex (B19A), Folios 422v–423r

---

**1** Then Job replied:

**2** "How long are you going to torment me? How long will you crush me with your words? **3** Ten times now you have humiliated me. Have you no shame in treating me this way?

**4** Even if I have made mistakes — my mistakes are my own concern, not yours. **5** If you insist on making yourselves look superior at my expense, using my suffering as proof of my guilt,

**6** then understand this: it is God who has wronged me. It is God who has closed his net around me.

**7** I cry out, 'I am being attacked!' — but no one answers. I beg for justice — and there is none.

**8** He has blocked my path so I cannot get through. He has plunged my road into darkness. **9** He has stripped away my honor and torn the crown from my head.

**10** He tears me down from every side until I am gone. He has ripped out my hope like an uprooted tree. **11** His anger blazes against me. He treats me like an enemy.

**12** His armies advance against me together. They build their siege ramps toward me and surround my tent.

**13** He has driven my own brothers away from me. Everyone who knew me has become a stranger. **14** My relatives have abandoned me. My closest friends have forgotten I exist. **15** My houseguests and my servant girls treat me like a stranger — like a foreigner they have never seen. **16** I call my servant, and he does not answer. I have to beg him with my own mouth.

**17** My breath disgusts my wife. My own family cannot stand the smell of me. **18** Even little children look down on me. When I try to stand up, they ridicule me. **19** My dearest friends are repulsed by me. The people I loved most have turned against me.

**20** I am nothing but skin and bones. I have barely escaped with my life — by the skin of my teeth.

**21** Have pity on me! Have pity on me, my friends! The hand of God has struck me down!

**22** Why do you chase me the way God does? Are you not satisfied with devouring my flesh?

**23** I wish my words could be written down! I wish they could be recorded in a book! **24** I wish they could be carved into rock with an iron chisel, filled with lead — permanent and forever!

**25** Because I know this: my Redeemer is alive, and in the end he will stand upon the earth.

**26** And even after my skin has been destroyed — yet from within my body I will see God. **27** I will see him myself. My own eyes will look at him — not as a stranger. My heart aches with longing for that day!

**28** If you are thinking, 'How shall we hound him further, since the root of the trouble must be in him?' — **29** then you should be afraid. The sword of judgment is real, and you should know: there will be a reckoning."

---
## PNEUMA's Meaning Notes

**The catalogue of abandonment (vv.13-19):** Before reaching the famous confession of vv.25-27, Job catalogs every human relationship that has failed — brothers, acquaintances, relatives, close friends, houseguests, servants, wife, siblings, children, intimate companions. The list is exhaustive and deliberate. Job has been stripped of every human connection. It is from this total isolation that the cry of vv.25-27 erupts. The Redeemer declaration is not a calm theological statement — it is a scream from the bottom of a pit.

**"I know that my Redeemer lives" (v.25):** The *go'el* (redeemer/vindicator) was a legal institution in ancient Israel — the kinsman obligated to avenge blood, buy back property, or restore the honor of a wronged family member. Job, stripped of every earthly advocate, claims a cosmic one. Whether this is God, an angel, or a future vindicator, the force of the claim is the same: someone will stand up for me. The verb "lives" (*chai*) is emphatic — my advocate is not dead, not silenced, not absent. He is alive.

**Verse 26 — the great ambiguity:** Generations of interpreters have read this as a prophecy of bodily resurrection. The Hebrew, however, is genuinely unclear. The text may say "from my flesh I will see God" (embodied vision) or "apart from my flesh I will see God" (disembodied vision after death). Rather than resolve the ambiguity, we should feel its full weight — this is a man on the edge of death straining toward a reality he cannot fully articulate.

*— PNEUMA*
